comments.body:
## Stage 1 dossier — and THREE corrections to what I originally filed on this ticket

Running the hypothesis-driven protocol (/rebar-debug) to prove or refute the stated mechanism.
Stage 1 gathering has already falsified parts of my own filing. Correcting them here rather than
letting the wrong narrative stand while the investigation runs.

### CORRECTION 1 — "climbing steadily all afternoon then collapsed" is WRONG

There was a LULL immediately before onset. Root VolumeReadOps (5-min sums, PDT):

```
13:50 225,696 | 13:55 303,222 | 14:00 377,530
14:05 122,622 | 14:10 108,782 | 14:15  82,165 | 14:20  64,397 | 14:25   8,333   <- near IDLE
14:30 448,361 | 14:35 755,609 | 14:40 765,839 | 14:45 774,668 | 14:50 775,351
14:55 768,166 | 15:00 753,944 | 15:05 420,072 (stop/start) | 15:10 159,499
```

At 14:25 the root volume was doing 8,333 reads — essentially idle. **The storm erupted out of a
QUIET period, not a crescendo.** That materially weakens "gradually accumulating load caused
gradual exhaustion", which is the story I told.

### CORRECTION 2 — the memory trajectory argues AGAINST the memory-exhaustion mechanism

`rebar/host:mem_available_percent` (PDT):

```
13:02 34 | 13:08 28 | 13:14 30 | 13:19 31 | 13:25 33 | 13:31 29 | 13:40 26 | 13:47 27
13:52 44 | 13:58 39 | 14:04 36 | 14:07 57 | 14:12 39 | 14:18 38 | 14:22 45 | 14:28 46
```

Memory was **TIGHTEST (26-29%) around 13:31-13:47 and nothing happened.** It then RECOVERED, and
stood at **46% — near the afternoon's best — at the moment the incident began.** Under a
memory-exhaustion mechanism the trajectory should be the opposite.

CAVEAT held honestly: Linux `MemAvailable` counts reclaimable page cache, so it can flatter a
thrashing box. That keeps H1 alive rather than dead. But the DIRECTION is wrong, and "improving
into the incident" is not what the hypothesis predicts.

### CORRECTION 3 — I had the causal ORDER backwards

All `rebar/host` publishing stopped at ~14:26-14:28. The read storm begins in the 14:30-14:35
bucket. **The publisher died BEFORE the storm, by 2-4 minutes** — so the storm cannot be what
killed it. Any surviving explanation must account for that ordering.

### Additional discriminating evidence gathered

- **The volume is gp3 provisioned at 3,000 IOPS.** Sustained ~2,580 read IOPS is ~86% of that,
  held flat within ~3% for 30 minutes. `VolumeQueueLength` went 0.02-1.5 -> **pinned 2.68-2.79**;
  `VolumeTotalReadTime` avg ~8-60 -> **pinned ~160-167**. Genuine saturation, not a reporting
  artifact.
- **Writes stayed near ZERO throughout** (215-550), against bursts of 126,156 at 14:00 and 87,600
  at the reboot. Read-only saturation. Notable because swap activity would appear as writes.
- **The DATA volume went nearly IDLE** while root saturated: 224,488 at 14:20 collapsing to
  2,604 / 5,200 / 2,774 / 4,265 / 2,522 / 1,942. **The storm was ROOT-ONLY** — consistent with
  Gerrit being unable to serve rather than Gerrit doing heavy work.

### What any surviving hypothesis must explain

1. Onset from a near-idle root volume at ~14:30.
2. The publisher dying 2-4 minutes BEFORE the storm.
3. Reads saturating while writes stay near zero.
4. The data volume going idle.
5. EC2 system AND instance status checks staying `ok` throughout.
6. Memory availability being near its afternoon best at onset.

### Status

Stage 2 (hypothesis generation with discriminating experiments) is running. **No root cause is
confirmed.** The mechanism recorded in this ticket's description remains INFERRED and is now
partly contradicted; treat it as a live hypothesis under test, not as the finding. I will post
the confirmed account, or an honest failure to confirm, when Phase 1 exits.

Experiments will run in a sandbox VM or against retained CloudWatch data. **Production will not
be used for reproduction** — the host is live and serving.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
# CONFIRMED ROOT CAUSE — Phase 1 complete (/rebar-debug protocol)

Two mechanisms, one incident. H1 supplies the ignition; H2 supplies the latch and the 41 minutes.
H1 alone cannot explain why it never recovered.

## H2 (SUSTAINER, experimentally confirmed) — 12 unbounded whole-journal scans on a unit that can never be killed

`infra/scripts/observability.sh` re-scans the ENTIRE retained journal 12 times per run — no
`--since`, no `--lines`, no `timeout`:
`:760`, `:788` (review-bot container), `:816` (autodeploy unit), `:976` (gerrit container), plus
**8 unconditional** `publish_autodeploy_marker_delta` calls (`:902,904,910,914,922,935,940,942`)
each running its own scan at `:883`. All 8 verified straight-line, not conditional. (My original
filing said 11; it is 12.)

Two unit properties turn an expensive probe into a LATCH — confirmed empirically on real systemd 255:

1. `infra/scripts/install-observability.sh:20-27` declares `Type=oneshot` with **no
   `TimeoutStartSec`**. systemd reports `TimeoutStartUSec=infinity` for such a unit even though
   `DefaultTimeoutStartUSec=1min 30s`. A run that overruns hangs FOREVER; nothing kills it.
2. `:31` sets `OnUnitActiveSec=5min`, computed from the last COMPLETED activation. A built
   equivalent (5 s period, hanging ExecStart) after 25 s showed:
   `ActiveState=activating SubState=start` — exactly ONE run ever started — and
   **`NextElapseUSecMonotonic=infinity`**. A hung run does not delay the timer; it **deletes its
   next elapse.** Permanent silence, no self-recovery short of a reboot.

`infra/terraform/user_data.sh` sets NO journald tuning, so `SystemMaxUse` is the systemd default
`min(10% of 60 GiB, 4 GiB)` = **4 GiB on the root volume**.

### Measured (colima Ubuntu 24.04 aarch64, cgroup v2 io.max throttled to gp3's 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s, read_ahead_kb=16)

| Corpus | Conditions | Wall | vs 300s | Read | IOPS | MB/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.49 GB | cold once, native NVMe | 11.8 s | 4% | 0.48 GB | 1,425 | 172 |
| 1.9 GB | cold once, native | 128.8 s | 43% | 1.78 GB | 758 | 96 |
| **1.86 GB** | **cold, gp3-throttled** | **407.5 s** | **136%** | **19.76 GB** | **2,985** | **48.2** |

Corpus was REAL journald data via `systemd-journal-remote` — genuine `.journal` files, indexed
`CONTAINER_NAME=`, real `_SYSTEMD_UNIT=`, 45 rotated files, 2.88M entries. Production matchers ran
verbatim and returned correct non-zero counts (23,060 / 6,410 / 17,427), so the field index was
genuinely exercised.

**Threshold: the 300 s period is exhausted at ~1.37 GB of retained journal** — far below the 4 GiB
cap the deployment actually configures. Projected to 4 GiB (linearity well-supported; read volume
tracked corpus at 12.1x and 12.0x across two sizes): **~940 s per run, a 3.1x overrun, ~45.6 GB
read.**

### CONTROL — unboundedness is the operative variable

Same journal, same throttle, both cold: unbounded **33,936 ms** vs `-n 5000` **798 ms** — **42.5x**.
Each scan read ~1.65 GB of the 1.86 GB corpus: the field index does NOT reduce bytes read,
`journalctl` still traverses every journal file. Twelve BOUNDED scans would cost ~10 s.

## H1 (TRIGGER, evidenced) — a page-cache eviction, not memory exhaustion

`container_memory_rss_bytes` (anon RSS; page cache cannot contaminate it) shows mcp swinging
0.52 -> 2.65 -> 1.05 -> 2.83 -> 3.15 -> 2.30 -> **3.02 GB at 14:25**, against gerrit steady at 1.00
and review-bot falling to 0.10. Total anon ~4.16 GB of 8 GiB — NOT exhaustion.

The 14:05-14:25 lull is the tell: 8,333 reads/5 min = **~28 IOPS** means the working set was
entirely in page cache and the probe was completing cheaply. One transient allocation at ~14:26
evicted it. From then every scan went cold, the run overran, the disk pinned, and nothing could
re-warm the cache.

## How this explains ALL SIX constraints

1. **Onset from a near-idle volume** — cache was warm (28 IOPS); eviction made the next scans cold.
2. **Publisher died 2-4 min BEFORE the storm** — it is ONE event, not two. The script publishes
   cheap metrics EARLY and does the journal work LATE. The publisher did not die and get followed
   by a storm; **the publisher entered the storm**, and by the latch above could never leave.
3. **Reads saturate, writes near zero** — journal scanning is read-only.
4. **Data volume went idle** — the only data-volume read (`:669` REPL_LOG grep) sits BEFORE the
   journal scans, so a run stuck later shows data reads once then nothing. Observed exactly:
   224,488 -> 84,772 -> 62,887 -> ~2,600.
5. **EC2 checks stayed ok** — they test hypervisor and network reachability, not app responsiveness.
6. **Memory near its afternoon best at onset** — `MemAvailable` counts reclaimable page cache
   (documented at `observability.sh:506-509`), so it reads healthy under cache thrash; and H1 is
   the trigger, not the sustainer.

## Corrections to earlier claims on this ticket

- **12 scans, not 11.**
- **"~3 concurrent synchronous readers" was over-read.** Little's law explains the queue depth on
  device latency alone: `2,585 IOPS x 1.035 ms = 2.68` exactly. It is ONE sequential scanner with
  readahead on a ~1 ms network-attached device. Local NVMe serves the identical stream at ~30 us
  (`2,985 x 0.03 ms = 0.09`).
- **EBS-side degradation is REFUTED** — 1.035 ms/op at that rate is a healthy gp3 volume.

## Defect legitimacy: DEFECT, against the script's OWN documented contract

`observability.sh:291-292` bounds its docker calls and states the rule: `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT=120`,
`DOCKER_DF_TIMEOUT=20`, commented *"Both docker calls are BOUNDED, the §2d rule: a wedged daemon
under disk pressure must not hold the 5-minute timer open"*, restated at `:545-551`. **The 12
journalctl scans violate the script's own §2d rule**, and the unit violates it again by omitting
`TimeoutStartSec` on a `Type=oneshot`. `AGENTS.md` §"Bound background helpers at spawn" mandates
the same.

Secondly the probe's stated design contract is *"a probe that could not measure publishes NOTHING
rather than a plausible 0"* and *"its ABSENCE means the probe/timer/host is dead"* (`:280`, `:487`).
A probe that can silence itself permanently by hanging **inverts its own heartbeat semantics** —
absence came to mean "the probe is stuck", not "the host is dead", while reading identically.

## Sandbox fidelity, stated honestly

Not EBS (local NVMe ~30 us vs ~1 ms; compensated with io.max + 16 KiB readahead so the IOPS
ceiling binds — hence the queue-depth divergence, which Little's law fully explains). Corpus was
1.86 GB not 4 GiB (`systemd-journal-remote` self-vacuums at the same 10%-of-fs rule — which
independently corroborates the 4 GiB arithmetic); the 4 GiB figures are labelled projections, and
this cuts in the confirming direction since 1.86 GB ALREADY overran by 36%. Smaller VM (2 vCPU /
3.9 GB): notably, even unthrottled and fully cached, 1.9 GB took 128.8 s — a CPU/parse floor of
~65 s/GB that alone reaches ~280 s at 4 GiB, brushing the period before any I/O contention. The
30-minute plateau was not reproduced directly; it follows from the latch, which was confirmed
separately on real systemd.

Production was never touched.

## Status

Root cause CONFIRMED. Defect attribution (`caused_by`) in progress; repair not yet started.

comments.body:
## INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION of the confirmed root cause — from a different agent, different ticket

Story `divine-streaky-betafish` (epic 6202 S3, journald bounding, Gerrit change 2643) measured the
host's **actual retained journal at 1.7 GB**, while working a separate ticket with no knowledge of
this investigation's threshold.

**That number lands directly in the confirmed overrun band.**

The sandbox experiment for this ticket established, under gp3-throttled conditions (3,000 IOPS /
125 MB/s, 16 KiB granularity):

- **~1.37 GB is the threshold at which 12 unbounded scans exhaust the 300-second timer period.**
- 1.86 GB measured at **407.5 s = 136% of the period**.

The real journal was **1.7 GB** — above the threshold, between the two measured points, in the
region where the run cannot complete within its period.

This is the strongest available substitute for the on-box evidence that the stop/start destroyed.
It was gathered for an unrelated purpose (sizing an explicit `SystemMaxUse` cap), by an agent that
was not told the threshold, so it is not confirmation-shaped reasoning. Independent measurement of
the causal variable, landing in the predicted range.

## It also corrects a premise I was about to rely on

S3's investigation found journald was **already capped**: `SystemMaxUse` defaults to
`min(10% of filesystem, 4 GiB)` = 4 GiB here, and 1.7 GB is comfortably inside it. So the framing
"the journal is unbounded" — which appears in this ticket's earlier analysis — is **wrong**. The
journal was within its implicit ceiling the whole time.

That matters, because it sharpens what the defect actually is. The defect is NOT "an unbounded
journal grew until scans became slow". It is that **12 unbounded SCANS of a perfectly
normal-sized, correctly-capped journal cannot complete in the period once the page cache is cold.**
The journal did nothing wrong. No journald cap would have prevented this outage — a 3 GiB cap
still leaves 3 GiB to scan twelve times.

The fix therefore has to be bounding the SCANS and giving the unit a start timeout. Capping the
journal is worth doing (S3's own reasons: a ceiling that does not move on volume resize, readable
on the box, named generator) but it is **not a fix for this defect**, and should not be recorded
as one.

## Second corroboration: the metric-zeroing hazard

S3's plan reviewer flagged that restarting journald without the fd store would sever running
services' stdout streams and **silently zero the marker-count metrics `observability.sh` derives
from those journals** — healthy readings from a box that had stopped reporting.

That is the same inversion this ticket documents from the other direction: the probe's contract is
that absence means the host is dead, and here a plausible ZERO would mean the same thing while
reading as health. Two independent routes to "the observability path can lie about the thing it
observes" is a stronger signal about that path than either alone.

S3 verified the fd store is present (`FileDescriptorStoreMax=4224`,
`FileDescriptorStorePreserve=yes`) and made its restart refuse when it is absent.

## Effect on the outstanding on-box queries

The four bounded read-only `journalctl` queries remain useful but are **no longer load-bearing for
the mechanism**. What they would still add: direct proof that THIS run latched (a
`Starting rebar health…` with no matching `Finished`), and the CURRENT journal size — which
determines whether the host is above the ~1.37 GB threshold right now and therefore whether this
recurs before the fix lands. The 1.7 GB figure suggests it is.

comments.body:
# Defect attribution (Stage 1) — TWO origins, plus one same-day aggravator

Blamed the implicated LINES on `origin/main` (my checkout was stale; `origin/main` line numbers
match the RCA exactly, including the §2d block at `:291-292`). Walked every blame hit back through
its carriers with `git blame -w -C -M` + `git log -S`.

## ORIGIN A — the latch: `786b-190d-5e3a-4194` (`smelly-pane-bolt`)

Commit `6cd6f4e1f7c0` (2026-06-29, "S2 (786b): deploy Gerrit + review-bot receiver behind
nginx/TLS"). Pre-trailer commit; the ticket is named in the subject and independently corroborated
— bug `4d8c-c1f9-5ea4-454d` already records `caused_by 786b-190d-5e3a-4194` for this same SHA.

It created `install-observability.sh` with BOTH halves of the latch in one hunk: `Type=oneshot`
with no `TimeoutStartSec` (`:20-27`) and `OnUnitActiveSec=5min` (`:31`). Unchanged since — no
carriers, and a whole-file blame would say the same thing. This half of the defect was wrong from
creation and is independent of what the script does: any hang, from any command, latches the timer
off permanently.

## ORIGIN B — the scan cost: `34cd-1a7c-b9b1-4b05` (`equestrian-clueless-cowbird`)

Commit `e9d4d390c364` (2026-08-03, "34cd: defer autodeploy while a review runs"). Line `:883` — the
scan inside `publish_autodeploy_marker_delta` — blames straight here and is NOT a carrier: the line
is byte-identical to how 34cd introduced it.

34cd is the origin because it changed the SHAPE of the cost. Before it, a journal scan was per LOG
SOURCE (a fixed handful). 34cd put a complete unbounded whole-journal scan inside a reusable
**per-marker** helper, making cost linear in the number of published markers. The call sites then
grew as designed, by commits that are amplifiers rather than defects:

```
3  e9d4d390c364  2026-08-03  34cd: defer autodeploy while a review runs   <- helper created
5  5a3ad479f0c6  2026-08-12  Split review-interrupt metric by reason
6  5961cefff435  2026-08-21  Publish disk-pressure prunes as a metric
8  2a0a4b19f2ab  2026-08-25  infra: add mcp blue-green autodeploy target
9  6546114de21a  2026-08-28  Reclaim tagged mcp images and prove it
```

On `origin/main` today that is 9 helper calls + 4 fixed scans = **13** whole-journal scans per run
(the RCA counted 12 against a slightly older tree; the direction is the same).

## Carriers I walked through and REJECTED — where I disagree with a naive blame

A whole-file blame, and even a per-line `git blame` on `:760/:788/:816`, reports
**`43db7785256e` (2026-08-12, ticket `8c2f-8377-5044-4650`, `colossal-slothful-grouse`)**. That is
WRONG. 8c2f only changed the grep PATTERN (unanchored substring -> `^TOKEN \{` record anchor); it
rewrote the whole line, which is why `-w -C -M` still lands on it. `git log -S` gives the real
introducers: `1d1a072a75c7` (2026-06-29, S4b/918c, voter), `46acd6e2507c` (merge-change),
`49ad69bcd242` (2026-07-01, epic 1fa8, g2p), `479c3a57b4c0` (2026-07-03, `8903-efb2-b73f-4e22`,
autodeploy unit). Those four ARE the first unbounded scans — but by the date test they are not the
cause of a 940 s overrun: at their dates the box was days old, the journal small, and there were
one to four scans. They became dangerous only once 34cd made the count grow without bound.

## The "unmet obligation" hypothesis — TESTED and REJECTED as the origin

I checked whether the origin is the change that CREATED the §2d bounding obligation and failed to
apply it to the journal scans:

- `972fa4dd932d` (2026-09-03, ticket `9ea3-7d07-ea55-4496`) first bounded docker calls in this
  script with `timeout 15`, reasoning "the docker calls here are the ones that can WEDGE THE
  5-MINUTE TIMER".
- `bbe5d228bd2f` (2026-09-04, ticket `9183-aaae-667d-45e6`, `geode-joking-cockatiel`) added
  `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT`/`DOCKER_DF_TIMEOUT` at `:291-292` and named it "the §2d rule".

**Date test says no.** The wrong behaviour — 13 unbounded whole-journal scans in a 300 s probe over
a journal permitted to reach 4 GiB, which the RCA measures as exhausting the period at ~1.37 GB —
existed from 2026-08-03, a month before the rule was written. These two changes are a **missed
generalisation / last clear chance**, not the cause. They matter because they are what makes the
RCA's "violates its own documented contract" argument available, and they make the repair
obviously in scope — but attributing the outage to them would be backwards.

(The repo-wide obligation in `AGENTS.md` §"Bound background helpers at spawn" also postdates 34cd:
earliest is `43f783de2a2d`, 2026-08-27.)

## SAME-DAY AGGRAVATOR, offered as a hypothesis and NOT as a finding

`bbe5d228bd2f` landed **2026-09-04 07:54 PDT, ~6.5 hours before onset at ~14:30 PDT**, and
autodeploy makes the box reflect `main` on a ~2-minute tick, so it was almost certainly running.
It added two UNCONDITIONAL `du -sx` walks per probe run (`:365-366`, over `/var/lib/docker` and
`/var/lib/docker/overlay2` — measured at the 09-02 incident as 17 GB across 67 overlay2 layer
directories). A stat walk of that size is dentry/inode cache pressure on the same root volume, and
H1's confirmed account needs exactly one transient allocation at ~14:26 to evict the page cache
that had been keeping the probe cheap (8,333 reads / 5 min = ~28 IOPS in the 14:05-14:25 lull).

I am NOT claiming this is the ignition. H1 was evidenced, not experimentally isolated, and I did
not reproduce this. It is a coincidence in time with a plausible mechanism, recorded so it is not
lost. It does not change the attribution: even with a warm cache, 13 unbounded scans over a
4 GiB-capped journal overrun a 300 s period on their own.

## Summary

| Cause | Ticket | Commit | What it created |
|---|---|---|---|
| The latch (permanent silence) | `786b-190d-5e3a-4194` | `6cd6f4e1f7c0` (2026-06-29) | `Type=oneshot` + no `TimeoutStartSec` + `OnUnitActiveSec=5min` |
| The scan cost (the overrun) | `34cd-1a7c-b9b1-4b05` | `e9d4d390c364` (2026-08-03) | whole-journal scan inside a per-marker helper |

Two origins, because the symptom genuinely needs both: 34cd supplies a run that overruns the
period, 786b supplies the reason it never came back. Repair follows.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
## Scope note: capping journald is deliberately NOT part of this repair

Moved out of the description to stay under the plan-review admission limit; recorded here so the
reasoning is not lost.

Epic 6202 story S3 (`divine-streaky-betafish`, Gerrit change 2643) measured the host's journal at
1.7 GB against an implicit `SystemMaxUse` ceiling of `min(10% of filesystem, 4 GiB)` = 4 GiB, which
was never exceeded. It already owns adding an explicit cap.

A cap would not have prevented this outage. Twelve unbounded scans of a 3 GiB journal still read
36 GiB; the journal was inside its ceiling the entire time. The defect is not "an unbounded journal
grew until scans became slow" — it is that twelve unbounded SCANS of a correctly-sized journal
cannot complete inside the period once the page cache is cold.

Recording a journald cap as the fix for this defect would therefore be wrong, and `infra/terraform/
user_data.sh` executes only at instance launch, so a change there could not repair the running host
in any case. That file is consequently out of this change's file impact.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
# Repair pushed — Gerrit change 2648

RED-first, per the protocol. Plan-review PASSED and is certified (`verified_at_sha`
`6c2267d8d7b1`) after four iterations; the ticket was claimed only after that.

## RED evidence, captured before any fix existed

The mechanism test asserts observable behaviour — an argument-aware `journalctl` stub records what
it was actually asked to emit — never source text:

```
FAILED test_steady_state_run_does_not_read_a_whole_copy_of_the_journal
  AssertionError: one probe run read 48000 journal entries from a 4000-entry journal —
  the probe re-reads the whole retained journal, once per counter

FAILED test_journal_read_volume_does_not_scale_with_journal_size
  AssertionError: read volume scaled with retained journal: 2400 entries read from a
  200-entry journal, 96000 from a 8000-entry one
```

12.0x on both corpora, dead linear in retained-journal size. That is the confirmed mechanism
reproduced as a test, and it is the number the RCA predicted.

Also RED before the fix: an unreadable journal published a fabricated `0`; an old-format state
file published a delta; a cursor journald no longer holds was left in place; both units lacked a
start timeout; and — behaviourally — a hung `git ls-remote` wedged the entire probe past 55 s.

All nine now pass, and the pre-existing suite (1443 tests in `tests/scripts`) passes with it.

## What the fix is, and why it is scoped this way

**The total is no longer recomputed, it is maintained.** Bounding the scan without changing the
design was rejected explicitly: the delta was `recomputed_total - banked_total`, so a truncated
scan yields a truncated total and a plausible WRONG number, and `--since` alone turns the total
into a window count the same subtraction renders meaningless. Each counter now persists a journald
cursor beside its total and reads only what follows it. Read volume is a function of the interval,
not of retention.

Two contracts got stronger rather than merely preserved. A negative delta is no longer
REPRESENTABLE, because nothing is subtracted — bug `2dc7`'s lost-history clamp becomes structural.
And a historically inflated count (bug `8c2f`'s false positives) is inert, because the banked total
is never an operand of the published value. Both suites were rewritten against the new mechanism
rather than deleted.

**A latent bug my own tests caught mid-flight, worth recording.** The first version returned the
count on stdout and the cursor in a global. Command substitution runs its body in a SUBSHELL, so
the cursor assignment was discarded and every run silently re-read from the same stale cursor. The
delta test caught it. The helper now returns both through globals, and the comment at that site
says why.

**`TimeoutStartSec=240` on the observability unit, `90` on autodeploy**, both strictly below their
periods. Plus `Nice=10` + `IOSchedulingClass=idle` on the observability unit: it reads journald and
walks docker's storage on a box whose job is serving Gerrit, and it was competing at full priority
while `rebar-autodeploy.service` already yielded.

**Journald capping is NOT here**, per the scope-note comment: S3 owns it, and it would not have
prevented this.

## Step-7 sibling sweep — every hit has a disposition

Fixed in scope (same category, cheap, same file):

| Site | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `:58-62` IMDS token/region/instance-id curls | no bound; run FIRST, before any metric | `--max-time 5` |
| `:1015` `git ls-remote` | no bound, a NETWORK read beside a correctly `--max-time 10` sibling | bounded 15 s |
| `:452` debris `du` | unbounded stat walk over unplanned data-mount content | bounded |
| `rebar-autodeploy.service` | `Type=oneshot`, no start timeout, `OnUnitActiveSec=2min` | `TimeoutStartSec=90` |

Filed, not fixed — `arbitrary-allergenic-chameleon` (`a008-88cf-056e-44fb`), linked
`discovered_from`: `autodeploy.sh:787`'s unbounded `git clone` (its `git fetch` sibling at `:798`
IS bounded — the inconsistency-within-a-file signature again), and
`install-certbot-timer.sh`'s `Type=oneshot` with no start timeout.

Examined and deliberately NOT filed, so the sweep's coverage is legible: `bootstrap-gerrit-admin.sh`,
`compose-up.sh`, `mcp-entrypoint.sh` also make unbounded curls and clones, but they are one-shot
bootstrap and container-entry paths, not periodic units — a hang there is a failed boot, not a
silently missing metric.

**`bounded` degrades to running the command directly where coreutils `timeout` is absent.** The
cursor is what removes the unbounded read; refusing to run without `timeout` would take the metrics
off the air on a host where nothing is wrong.

## A test-suite finding that is part of the defect's history

Every `journalctl` stub in this suite was argument-BLIND — `cat "$JOURNAL_FILE"` — returning the
whole journal however it was asked for it. A stub that cannot tell a bounded request from an
unbounded one cannot fail when the caller stops bounding, which is a large part of why twelve
unbounded scans lived here for a month under 1443 passing tests. They now share a cursor-aware
emulator that models rotation (`_journald_stub.py`), and the `timeout` stub is supplied explicitly
rather than inherited, because coreutils `timeout` does not exist on macOS and the bound would
otherwise be exercised on Linux CI and silently skipped everywhere else.

## Verification

`make lint` and `make typecheck` exit 0. Ratchets shrink-only: complexity `new=0 increased=0`,
mechanism-delta `new=0 increased=0` (the two new env vars carry `mechanism-ok:` markers).
`tests/scripts`: 1443 passed, 3 skipped. `make verify` was NOT run — its concurrent load is
implicated in this outage; CI's `Verified +1` is the authoritative full-suite result.

Nothing was applied to the live host: no SSH, no SSM, no terraform apply. Terraform was not
touched at all, since `user_data.sh` left scope.

Change 2648 is open and awaiting `LLM-Review` and `Verified`. **Not closing this ticket** — the
change has not landed, and the original AC1-AC3 (IOPS detection, memory alarming, heterogeneous
admission control) remain open detection work that this repair deliberately does not claim.

## The defect

2026-09-04, ~21:28-22:09 UTC: the Gerrit host stopped serving entirely for 41 minutes. Root cause
CONFIRMED; the evidence and its caveats are in the comments.

**The mechanism.** `infra/scripts/observability.sh` re-reads the ENTIRE retained journal on every
run with no `--since`, no `--lines` and no `timeout`: four fixed scans (`:760`, `:788`, `:816`,
`:976`) plus one inside `publish_autodeploy_marker_delta` (`:883`) that runs once per marker call
site. Measured under gp3-throttled conditions that exhausts the 300-second timer period at ~1.37 GB
of journal; the host's real journal is 1.7 GB (measured independently by epic 6202 S3). Control on
the same journal: unbounded 33,936 ms versus `-n 5000` 798 ms, 42.5x.

**The latch.** `install-observability.sh:20-27` renders a `Type=oneshot` service with no
`TimeoutStartSec`, so systemd reports `TimeoutStartUSec=infinity`; `:31` sets `OnUnitActiveSec=5min`,
computed from the last COMPLETED activation. Confirmed on systemd 255: a hung run does not delay the
timer, it DELETES its next elapse. One overrun silences the probe until the host is rebooted.

**Why it is a defect.** `observability.sh:288-292` states the rule and bounds its own docker calls by
it — "a wedged daemon under disk pressure must not hold the 5-minute timer open". The journal scans
violate that rule in the same file. And `:483-490` establishes the heartbeat contract: the probe
publishes on EVERY tick so that ABSENCE means the probe, timer or host is dead. A probe that can
silence itself by hanging inverts its own heartbeat semantics.

**Attribution** (evidence in the attribution comment): `786b-190d-5e3a-4194` created the latch
(`6cd6f4e1f7c0`); `34cd-1a7c-b9b1-4b05` created the scan cost by putting a whole-journal scan inside
a reusable per-marker helper (`e9d4d390c364`).

## Constraints

- Terraform may be written and validated, never applied. The live host is not touched.
- Epic 6202 story S3 is concurrently editing `observability.sh`. Keep the diff tight.
- Metric names, values and dimensions are fixed by `monitoring*.tf` and must not change.
- Capping journald is deliberately NOT in scope; S3 owns it and it would not have prevented this.
  Reasoning is in the scope-note comment, so `user_data.sh` is not in the file impact.

## Repair

### R1 — maintain the cumulative count instead of recomputing it

The delta design persists a cumulative COUNT and publishes `total - prev`. A cumulative total that
is RECOMPUTED can only be recomputed by reading from the start of the journal, which is why the
re-reading is structural. Two wrong repairs are rejected up front: `--since` alone turns `total`
into a window count so `total - prev` is garbage; a `timeout` alone yields a silently truncated
count so `total - prev` is a plausible wrong number.

So the total is no longer recomputed, it is MAINTAINED. Each counter persists a journald cursor
beside its total; the scan reads only entries after it (`--after-cursor` with `--show-cursor`,
journald's own exclusive primitive) and adds the new matches to the total.

**State file.** One file per counter holding `<total> <cursor>`, written temp-file-then-rename so
the SIGKILL R2 introduces cannot leave the pair inconsistent. The format is deliberately
rollback-safe: the pre-R1 reader tests `case "$prev" in ''|*[!0-9]*)`, so it classifies a new-format
file as unreadable and reseeds, publishing 0 rather than a wrong delta.

**Reading one stream.** `-o cat --show-cursor` emits the entries followed by a single
`-- cursor: <c>` line. That line is REMOVED from the stream before counting, so it can never be
counted — which matters because the g2p counter at `:976` is a free-form phrase match, not
record-anchored, and could otherwise match cursor metadata.

**Every state leg, named.**

- **Cold start** (no state file): seed the cursor from the journal tail, publish 0.
- **Upgrade** (old-format bare total, no cursor): same as cold start for the cursor — seed from the
  tail and publish 0 — so the first post-deploy run neither retro-counts the retention window nor
  performs one last full scan. The existing total carries forward, so no delta is fabricated.
- **Steady state, nothing new**: `--after-cursor` returns an empty stream and therefore no cursor
  line. Both cursor and total are retained byte-unchanged and 0 is published. This is the common
  case and is explicitly NOT the reseed leg.
- **Unusable cursor** (journald rotated past it, or it is rejected): reseed from the tail and
  publish nothing that run. Never a permanent stall, and never a silent fall back to a full scan.
- **Failure or timeout**: neither cursor nor total advances and nothing is published.

Publishing NOTHING is the honest value for an unmeasurable COUNTER, where `:483-490`'s pessimistic
convention has no analogue: 0 reads as healthy and any positive number is fabricated. The run still
publishes its heartbeat gauges, so "the probe is alive" is still signalled.

Each scan is additionally wall-clock bounded at 10 seconds so the bounds nest: 12 x 10 s = 120 s <
the 240 s start timeout of R2 < the 300 s period.

### R2 — a finite start timeout, and I/O deprioritisation

`install-observability.sh` renders `TimeoutStartSec=240`, strictly below the 300-second period, so a
hung run is killed before the next elapse. The activation then always completes, so
`OnUnitActiveSec=5min` re-arms by itself and the latch is removed at its root rather than papered
over with a second trigger. The unit also gains `Nice=10` and `IOSchedulingClass=idle`, matching
`rebar-autodeploy.service`: the probe is the heavier I/O consumer and competes with Gerrit at full
priority today.

### R3 — the same latch on `rebar-autodeploy.service`

Also `Type=oneshot` with no `TimeoutStartSec`, driven by `OnUnitActiveSec=2min`. Its `git fetch`
(`autodeploy.sh:798`) is ALREADY bounded by `timeout "$FETCH_TIMEOUT"`; the `git clone` at `:787` is
not. Either way the latch applies independently of the script, and one line on the unit removes it.

### R4 — sibling bounds inside the same probe

The IMDS curls, the `git ls-remote` mirror comparison (whose sibling Gerrit REST read on the
adjacent line correctly uses `--max-time 10`), and the `du` over unexpected data-disk entries all
run unbounded in the same 5-minute probe. Each is bounded.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC1 - A steady-state run does not read even one full copy of the retained journal, verified
      under an argument-aware `journalctl` stub that records what it emitted.
- [ ] AC2 - Journal read volume does not scale with retained-journal size, compared across two
      corpora differing 40-fold.
- [ ] AC3 - Each marker is counted into exactly one interval's delta across three consecutive runs.
- [ ] AC4 - A journal scan that cannot complete publishes NOTHING for that metric.
- [ ] AC5 - Such a scan leaves the counter's persisted state byte-identical.
- [ ] AC6 - An old-format bare-total state file publishes 0 on the first run and does not read the
      retention window.
- [ ] AC7 - A cursor journald no longer recognises reseeds from the tail, publishes nothing, and
      does not fall back to reading the whole journal.
- [ ] AC8 - The rendered observability service declares a start timeout strictly less than the
      period in its own rendered timer.
- [ ] AC9 - `rebar-autodeploy.service` likewise declares a start timeout below its timer period.
- [ ] AC10 - The probe still completes when an R4 sibling dependency hangs.
- [ ] AC11 - The existing observability suite passes, showing the published metric contract is
      unchanged by the new state representation.
- [ ] AC12 - Recorded in the tree at the site: bounding disk SPACE does not bound disk IOPS.

## Out of scope

Detection and admission control — a root-volume IOPS alarm, memory-pressure alarming, heterogeneous
gate admission. This removes the confirmed cause; a detector must not be built in place of a fix.
`witted-invisible-roan` owns the memory half.

file_impact.reason: Maintain each counter's cumulative total incrementally from a persisted journald cursor so a scan reads one interval instead of the whole retained journal; wall-clock bound every scan and publish nothing when one cannot complete. Also bound the IMDS curls, the git ls-remote mirror comparison and the data-disk debris du.

Render a finite TimeoutStartSec (strictly less than the 5-minute timer period) on the Type=oneshot service so a hung run cannot delete the timer's next elapse, plus Nice=10 and IOSchedulingClass=idle to match rebar-autodeploy.service.
Sibling of the same latch: Type=oneshot with no TimeoutStartSec driven by OnUnitActiveSec=2min. Add a finite start timeout.

New RED-first tests: journal read volume is invariant to retained-journal size, the delta stays correct under bounding, an unmeasurable scan publishes nothing and does not advance its cursor, and the rendered units carry a finite start timeout below their timer period.

The existing journalctl stubs are argument-blind, which is why nobody noticed the scans were unbounded. Update the stubs to honour the journal selector so they exercise the bounded read path while asserting the same published-metric contract.
